evidence_quotes.quote: Hygienic/safe emptying was practiced by 52.3% of households in the study area, mainly relying on mechanical methods using vacuum trucks.

The interviews with institutional stakeholders focused mainly on the socio-economic and environmental determinants of emptying practices, as well as the regulatory mechanisms that govern those practices.

evidence_quotes.quote: In addition, among the community members interviewed, some argued that the cost of emptying is not well regulated, and the rates charged by emptying companies are beyond the reach of most households, who already struggle to pay the sanitation tax deducted from the water bill.

evidence_quotes.quote: In fact, the likelihood of unhygienic/unsafe emptying is extremely lower in households that own their own houses than in those where they do not (aOR = 0.27; 95% CI 0.15–0.47; p < 0.001).
A cross-sectional mixed study used in the municipality of Yopougon (Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire), involved surveys (559 household), and 24 semi-structured interviews.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to and uptake of formal hygienic/safe mechanical fecal sludge emptying services (vacuum trucks transporting sludge to designated dumping/treatment sites) versus unhygienic/unsafe alternatives (illegal pipe discharge to drains or manual emptying) in non-sewered areas of Yopougon, Abidjan.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study investigates institutional, legal, regulatory, and governance aspects of fecal sludge management (ONAD, municipal decentralization, the Water Code, municipal bylaws, and the Construction and Housing Code). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing service access and affordability: (1) housing tenure status (owner vs. tenant, aOR = 0.27, 95% CI 0.15–0.47, p < 0.001) linked to statutory landlord-tenant obligations to construct and empty on-site sanitation facilities under Articles 268 and 431 of Law n2019-576; (2) tariff and cost-recovery rules (absence of regulated emptying tariffs for private vacuum-truck operators alongside a mandatory sanitation tax deducted from household water bills); and (3) regulatory enforcement rules and municipal penalties (Water Code Articles 48, 49, and 51; Yopougon Municipal Declaration N2014-02/C.Yop/SG imposing a 59 USD fine, and enforcement failure tied to unfunded decentralization), assessed empirically via 24 stakeholder interviews and household surveys.
criterion_notes.c3: Cross-sectional mixed-methods primary empirical study combining a stratified random survey of 559 households (n = 359 in multivariate logistic regression), GIS morphological analysis, and thematic content analysis of 24 semi-structured stakeholder interviews.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household uptake/use of formal hygienic/safe mechanical emptying services (52.3%) versus unhygienic/unsafe emptying practices (47.6%: 38.1% illegal pipe discharge and 9.5% manual emptying; binary outcome in logistic regression) as well as qualitative affordability barriers to accessing formal mechanical emptying.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (households served by non-sewered sanitation in Yopougon municipality, Abidjan, n = 559 surveyed / n = 359 in regression; plus n = 24 institutional, service-provider, and community informants), exposures (housing tenure, income, spatial variables, tariff regulation/water-bill sanitation tax, and regulatory enforcement), outcome (safe mechanical vs. unsafe fecal sludge emptying practice and affordability), and study design (cross-sectional mixed-methods).

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods study (stratified random household survey with logistic regression, GIS spatial analysis, and semi-structured stakeholder interviews with thematic content analysis)
population_and_sample: Households using non-sewered on-site sanitation in Yopougon municipality, Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire (n = 559 surveyed households across four housing strata; n = 380 had emptied pits/tanks; n = 359 with complete data in logistic regression; unit of analysis: household) and n = 24 institutional, service-provider, and community stakeholders interviewed
exposure: Housing tenure status (homeowner vs. tenant under statutory landlord sanitation obligations in Law n2019-576), tariff and cost-recovery rules (unregulated vacuum-truck emptying rates alongside a mandatory water-bill sanitation tax), regulatory enforcement of national/municipal emptying rules and fines, household income, and spatial/environmental proximity to water bodies and gullies
outcome: Household use of hygienic/safe mechanical fecal sludge emptying service (vacuum truck) versus unhygienic/unsafe emptying (illegal pipe discharge or manual emptying), and perceived service affordability
rationale: This cross-sectional mixed-methods study in Yopougon, Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Quantitatively, it estimates the association between household tenure (homeownership vs. tenancy, aOR = 0.27 for unsafe vs. safe mechanical emptying) and uptake of formal mechanical fecal sludge emptying services among 359 households, linking tenure disparities to statutory landlord obligations under the Construction and Housing Code. Qualitatively, through 24 stakeholder interviews analyzed via thematic content analysis, it directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing service access and affordability: lack of tariff regulation for private emptying trucks coupled with a sanitation tax deducted on water bills, and non-enforcement of national Water Code provisions and municipal fines due to unfunded decentralization.
